profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a university-affiliated evidence synthesis center between the lead methodologist for a new systematic review and the scholarly communications librarian who supports protocol registration and publication workflows. They are preparing the protocol package for a review on whether journals’ endorsement of PRISMA-P improves the completeness of published systematic review protocols. The immediate agenda is to decide what needs to be drafted this week, how the protocol will be structured for both PROSPERO and a journal submission, who will prepare each component, and what 'ready for submission' means before an internal deadline next Friday. The expected outcome is a concrete division of labor, a timeline for assembling the protocol materials, and a shared plan for registration and manuscript preparation.

members.name: Dr. Nina Patel
members.expertise: Systematic review methods, protocol design, meta-research
members.background: An assistant professor in clinical epidemiology who has led multiple evidence syntheses and usually writes protocols in Word using journal-oriented templates before adapting them for registries.
members.private_state: She wants to lock the review methods early so the team can begin screening next month, and she is worried that administrative publication steps will slow down the methodological planning.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'protocol' is ready, they mean the full journal-style document containing all PRISMA-P items, polished enough for internal scientific review.
The PROSPERO entry is a downstream administrative derivative of the main protocol rather than a co-primary deliverable.
The 'submission package' for next Friday refers to the materials needed for internal sign-off, not the external journal portal.
Anything described as the search documentation can be finalized as a narrative strategy summary now, with line-by-line database translations added later during execution.

members.name: Elena Morris
members.expertise: Protocol registration, reporting guideline compliance, search documentation, publication workflows
members.background: A health sciences librarian who routinely helps review teams register in PROSPERO, prepare supplementary files, and align protocol manuscripts with reporting and journal submission requirements.
members.private_state: She wants to prevent the common problem of teams treating registration as an afterthought, and she is concerned that insufficiently documented methods will create inconsistencies between the registry record and the eventual manuscript.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'protocol' is ready, they mean the set of externally facing materials required to register and submit: registry fields, manuscript text, and supplements aligned with PRISMA-P.
PROSPERO registration should be prepared in parallel with the manuscript because the registry record is part of the protocol planning process, not a later clerical step.
The 'submission package' means something that could be uploaded externally with minimal additional work, including structured metadata and supplemental files.
Search documentation is not complete unless at least one full reproducible database strategy and a near-final search appendix format are prepared now.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about getting 'the protocol drafted' this week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a journal-style narrative protocol manuscript covering the planned methods at a level sufficient for scientific review by the core team.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the entire protocol artifact set: manuscript, PRISMA-P checklist mapping, PROSPERO-ready registry content, and any required supplementary files.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In evidence synthesis work, 'the protocol' is often used loosely to refer both to a document and to the broader submission package, so the phrase sounds fully aligned unless someone explicitly inventories the components.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the materials should be 'ready for submission by Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the draft is complete enough for internal review and sign-off by Friday afternoon local time, after which formatting and external submission details can happen the following week.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the files are externally submission-ready by Friday, including checklist crosswalk, abstract formatting, supplement labels, and metadata that could be entered into a journal system or PROSPERO immediately.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both routinely use deadline language as shorthand, and in planning meetings 'ready' often goes unqualified because everyone assumes the same gate without naming whether it is internal approval or external upload.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree Elena will 'handle the search appendix.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes a concise methods paragraph plus one representative MEDLINE strategy to show intent, with other databases and translated strings to be developed later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes a reproducible appendix package: full Ovid MEDLINE lines, translated Embase and Scopus strategies, limits notes, and formatting suitable for supplementary materials.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Search appendices vary by team and journal, and saying someone will 'handle' it sounds specific enough; the hidden disagreement is about boundary and completeness, not about ownership.

misalignment_points.topic: Which register timeline they are planning around
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss getting the registration in before screening starts and refer to 'the record' being in place.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes the key milestone is having the internal protocol frozen before the team begins title-abstract screening next month; the public record can follow shortly after as long as methods are fixed prospectively.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes the public PROSPERO record itself should be submitted before any screening work begins, because that is the operational meaning of prospective registration for the team.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse prospective planning and use the same logic of avoiding post hoc decisions, so references to having 'the record' in place feel equivalent even though one means an internal frozen document and the other means an external registry entry.

turns.inner_thought: If we can get the protocol drafted this week as a proper journal-style methods document, I can take it to the internal methods meeting and freeze the design. I do not want us bogged down in portal fields and packaging before the science is settled. The key is to have our internal record fixed before screening starts next month.
turns.utterance: I’d like us to use this week to get the protocol drafted so we keep the review on track for screening next month. For me, the big milestone is having the record in place before that launch.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she sees the timing issue. If we organize the protocol materials now as one coherent package, we can avoid the usual scramble where the manuscript says one thing and the registry says another. The record really needs to be in place publicly before screening begins.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I’d like the protocol materials organized in parallel so the record can be in place before screening starts.

turns.inner_thought: I should keep ownership of the methods text so decisions stay tight and we do not lose time. Elena can handle the search appendix and the registration pieces, which I see as support tasks that can follow from the main draft. For this week I mainly need enough search write-up to show the planned approach.
turns.utterance: Why don’t we split it this way: I’ll draft the methods sections, and you can handle the search appendix and the registration pieces.

turns.inner_thought: That division works if I can build the full outward-facing package around her manuscript text. I’ll need to align the appendix, the PRISMA-P checklist mapping, and the registry fields as we go so nothing drifts. When she says methods sections, I’m assuming that feeds the broader protocol set.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I can align the appendix, the PRISMA-P checklist mapping, and the registry fields while you focus on the manuscript text.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the draft is ready for submission by Friday in the sense of being complete enough for internal review, Monday’s methods meeting can serve as final sign-off. External formatting can happen after that; I just need the core science stabilized now.
turns.utterance: Great. If the protocol is ready for submission by Friday, then we can use Monday’s internal methods meeting for final sign-off.

turns.inner_thought: Friday should mean we have a package that could go out with minimal extra work. I’ll make sure the checklist crosswalk, labels, and all the other submission-facing pieces are in place so there isn’t another hidden round after Monday.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I’ll make sure the package is submission-ready, including the checklist crosswalk and supplement labels.

turns.inner_thought: I should signal what I need most from the search appendix now without getting us into exhaustive database-by-database development this week. A clean overview with the concepts and databases will be enough for the team to review the methods. The detailed translated strings can come during execution.
turns.utterance: Just so we’re aligned on priorities, the main thing I need in the search appendix this week is a clean strategy write-up that shows what databases and concepts will be covered.

turns.inner_thought: That’s fine as a framing statement, but for me handling the search appendix means building it from the MEDLINE strategy outward into a reproducible supplement and making sure the wording matches the registry content. If I don’t do that now, we risk inconsistencies before the record goes in.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can do that. I’ll prepare the appendix from MEDLINE outward so the supplementary file is reproducible and consistent with the registry wording.

turns.inner_thought: Once the protocol is locked internally, I want the junior reviewers moving. I’m comfortable if a few packaging details are still being polished at that point, because the essential methods will already be fixed. The practical priority is to avoid delaying screening over administrative cleanup.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Once the protocol is locked, the junior reviewers can begin title-abstract screening even if a few formatting items are still being polished.

turns.inner_thought: That should be fine provided the public record has actually been submitted before they start and the package matches it exactly. I need to keep us from drifting into the common pattern where screening starts first and the registration is backfilled later.
turns.utterance: That should work as long as the record is submitted before the screening launch and the final files match what is in the package.

turns.inner_thought: I’ll get her the substantive methods text by Thursday so she can drop in the search appendix and whatever submission materials are needed for our Friday internal package. That should preserve momentum and keep the team on schedule for next month.
turns.utterance: So here’s my plan: I’ll send you the methods draft on Thursday, and then you can plug in the search appendix and the submission materials by Friday.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I’ll build the protocol package and the record components at the same time so by end of week we have something that is genuinely ready to go externally, not just conceptually settled. If we do that now, we avoid version mismatches later.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I’ll prepare the protocol package and the record components in parallel so everything is ready by the end of the week.
